claim: Various heterozygous cytoskeletal γ-actin mutations have been shown to cause Baraitser–Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome, non-syndromic hearing loss, or isolated eye coloboma.
source: Various heterozygous cytoskeletal γ-actin mutations have been shown to cause Baraitser–Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome, non-syndromic hearing loss, or isolated eye coloboma.
evidence: This is a general statement about known associations between γ-actin mutations and diseases, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The E334Q mutation in cytoskeletal γ-actin leads to a hitherto unspecified non-muscle actinopathy.
source: Here, we report the biochemical characterization of human cytoskeletal γ-actin carrying mutation E334Q, a mutation that leads to a hitherto unspecified non-muscle actinopathy.
evidence: This statement is based on the clinical observation of a patient with this mutation, as referenced in the manuscript.

claim: p.E334Q monomers show normal integration into linear and branched actin filaments.
source: Following expression, purification, and removal of linker and thymosin β4 tag sequences, the p.E334Q monomers show normal integration into linear and branched actin filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TIRF microscopy and pyrene-based polymerization assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The E334Q mutation does not affect thermal stability of actin.
source: The mutation does not affect thermal stability, actin filament nucleation, elongation, and turnover.
evidence: This is supported by DSF experiments showing similar denaturation temperatures for WT and mutant actin (Figure 1C, Table 1).

claim: The E334Q mutation does not affect actin filament nucleation.
source: The mutation does not affect thermal stability, actin filament nucleation, elongation, and turnover.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing similar nucleation rates for WT and mutant actin (Figure 2C).

claim: The E334Q mutation does not affect actin filament elongation.
source: The mutation does not affect thermal stability, actin filament nucleation, elongation, and turnover.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy showing only a small reduction in elongation rate (Figure 2B, Table 1).

claim: The E334Q mutation does not affect actin filament turnover.
source: The mutation does not affect thermal stability, actin filament nucleation, elongation, and turnover.
evidence: This is supported by steady-state ATPase measurements showing similar rates for WT and mutant filaments (Table 1).

claim: Model building and normal mode analysis predict significant differences in the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with myosin motors.
source: Model building and normal mode analysis predict significant differences in the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with myosin motors and members of the ADF/cofilin family of actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and structural analysis presented in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Model building and normal mode analysis predict significant differences in the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with members of the ADF/cofilin family of actin-binding proteins.
source: Model building and normal mode analysis predict significant differences in the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with myosin motors and members of the ADF/cofilin family of actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and structural analysis presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: p.E334Q filaments show significant reductions in sliding velocity with human class 2 myosin motor constructs.
source: Assays probing the interactions of p.E334Q filaments with human class 2 and class 5 myosin motor constructs show significant reductions in sliding velocity and actin affinity.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro motility assay data showing 5-fold reduction in sliding velocity with NM2A-HMM (Figure 8A, B, Table 1).

claim: p.E334Q filaments show significant reductions in sliding velocity with human class 5 myosin motor constructs.
source: Assays probing the interactions of p.E334Q filaments with human class 2 and class 5 myosin motor constructs show significant reductions in sliding velocity and actin affinity.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro motility assay data showing 1.7-fold reduction in sliding velocity with Myo5A-HMM (Figure 9, Table 1).

claim: p.E334Q filaments show significant reductions in actin affinity with human class 2 myosin motor constructs.
source: Assays probing the interactions of p.E334Q filaments with human class 2 and class 5 myosin motor constructs show significant reductions in sliding velocity and actin affinity.
evidence: This is supported by transient kinetic analysis showing 9.9-fold reduced affinity under rigor conditions (Figure 8E, Table 1).

claim: E334Q increases the rate of cofilin-mediated de novo nucleation of actin filaments.
source: E334Q differentially affects cofilin-mediated actin dynamics by increasing the rate of cofilin-mediated de novo nucleation of actin filaments and decreasing the efficiency of cofilin-mediated filament severing.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy experiments showing faster filament formation with p.E334Q in the presence of cofilin (Figure 4).

claim: E334Q decreases the efficiency of cofilin-mediated filament severing.
source: E334Q differentially affects cofilin-mediated actin dynamics by increasing the rate of cofilin-mediated de novo nucleation of actin filaments and decreasing the efficiency of cofilin-mediated filament severing.
evidence: This is supported by pyrene-based depolymerization assays and two-color TIRF microscopy showing reduced severing efficiency (Figures 5 and 6, Table 1).

claim: p.E334Q-mediated changes in myosin motor activity likely contribute to the observed disease phenotype.
source: Thus, it is likely that p.E334Q-mediated changes in myosin motor activity, as well as filament turnover, contribute to the observed disease phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing impaired myosin interactions and the known roles of myosins in cellular function.

claim: p.E334Q-mediated changes in filament turnover likely contribute to the observed disease phenotype.
source: Thus, it is likely that p.E334Q-mediated changes in myosin motor activity, as well as filament turnover, contribute to the observed disease phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing altered cofilin-mediated dynamics and the known importance of actin turnover in cellular processes.

claim: Cytoskeletal β- and γ-actin are the basic building blocks of the actin cytoskeleton in human non-muscle cells.
source: Cytoskeletal β- and γ-actin are the basic building blocks of the actin cytoskeleton in human non-muscle cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations (Pollard, 2016; Plastino and Blanchoin, 2018).

claim: β- and γ-actin differ by only four amino acids in the N-terminal region of the molecule.
source: β- and γ-actin differ by only four amino acids in the N-terminal region of the molecule but show isoform-specific spatial organization in studies performed with monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sequence differences between actin isoforms.

claim: β- and γ-actin show isoform-specific spatial organization in studies performed with monoclonal antibodies.
source: β- and γ-actin differ by only four amino acids in the N-terminal region of the molecule but show isoform-specific spatial organization in studies performed with monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using monoclonal antibodies (Dugina et al., 2009; Latham et al., 2013; Dugina et al., 2015).

claim: In motile and stationary cells, β-actin is found in contractile stress fibers and the cell periphery.
source: In motile and stationary cells, β-actin is found in contractile stress fibers and the cell periphery (Dugina et al., 2009; Latham et al., 2013; Dugina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: During cell movement, γ-actin is recruited to the leading edge of the cell, resulting in an enrichment of the isoform in the lamellipodium together with β-actin.
source: During cell movement, γ-actin is recruited to the leading edge of the cell, resulting in an enrichment of the isoform in the lamellipodium together with β-actin (Dugina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In non-moving cell states, γ-actin is co-localized with β-actin in stress fibers.
source: In non-moving cell states, γ-actin is co-localized with β-actin in stress fibers (Dugina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Baraitser–Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome (BWCFF) is a condition that affects the development of multiple organs, but particularly results in facial anomalies and brain malformations.
source: Baraitser–Winter cerebrontofacial syndrome (BWCFF, Baraitser and Winter, 1988) is a condition that affects the development of multiple organs, but particularly results in facial anomalies and brain malformations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BWCFF, supported by citations.

claim: BWCFF occurs due to various missense mutations in ACTB or ACTG1.
source: BWCFF occurs due to various missense mutations in ACTB or ACTG1 (Verloes et al., 2015; Di Donato et al., 2014; Rivière et al., 2012; Di Donato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Variants in ACTB generally result in a stronger facial phenotype than mutations in ACTG1 in BWCFF patients.
source: BWCFF patients show a recognizable facial gestalt, with variants in ACTB generally resulting in a stronger facial phenotype than mutations in ACTG1 (Di Donato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Residue E334 is located in the hinge region of the actin molecule.
source: Structural analysis of the disease-causing mutation shows that residue E334 is located in the hinge region of the actin molecule, which connects the two subdomain pairs of the protein.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is also shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The hinge region connects the two subdomain pairs of the actin protein.
source: Structural analysis of the disease-causing mutation shows that residue E334 is located in the hinge region of the actin molecule, which connects the two subdomain pairs of the protein.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about actin.

claim: The hinge region's flexibility and ability to act as a pivot point are essential for the subdomain rearrangement when actin monomers polymerize into filaments.
source: The region's flexibility and ability to act as a pivot point are essential for the subdomain rearrangement when actin monomers polymerize into filaments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin polymerization, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: E334 is part of a contact region on the F-actin surface that interacts with the cardiomyopathy loop in the motor domain of cytoskeletal myosin isoforms.
source: Furthermore, E334 is part of a contact region on the F-actin surface that interacts with the so-called cardiomyopathy loop in the motor domain of cytoskeletal myosin isoforms and contributes to the formation of the actin–cofilin complex (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: E334 contributes to the formation of the actin–cofilin complex.
source: Furthermore, E334 is part of a contact region on the F-actin surface that interacts with the so-called cardiomyopathy loop in the motor domain of cytoskeletal myosin isoforms and contributes to the formation of the actin–cofilin complex (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The patient carrying the E334Q mutation showed developmental delay and severe muscle hypotonia at 4 years of age.
source: At 4 y (age of diagnosis), a patient carrying this mutation showed developmental delay and severe muscle hypotonia (Di Donato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is clinical data from a published case report.

claim: The clinical phenotype of the patient with E334Q mutation cannot be classified as BWCFF and is therefore assigned as an unclassified NMA.
source: Although the patient was initially reported within the ACTG1-associated BWCFF cohort, careful reassessment of the phenotype revealed that the clinical phenotype cannot be classified as BWCFF and is therefore assigned as an unclassified NMA.
evidence: This is based on clinical reassessment referenced in the manuscript.

claim: The IC50 value of p.E334Q in the DNase I inhibition assay is 25.7 ± 0.6 nM.
source: We observed a 10% increase in the apparent IC50 value of p.E334Q (25.7 ± 0.6 nM) compared to the WT protein (22.7 ± 0.7 nM) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from DNase I inhibition assays shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: The IC50 value of WT γ-actin in the DNase I inhibition assay is 22.7 ± 0.7 nM.
source: We observed a 10% increase in the apparent IC50 value of p.E334Q (25.7 ± 0.6 nM) compared to the WT protein (22.7 ± 0.7 nM) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from DNase I inhibition assays shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: CD spectroscopy results show nearly identical secondary structure compositions for WT and mutant proteins.
source: This is in good agreement with circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy results showing nearly identical secondary structure compositions for WT and mutant proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The thermal denaturation temperature of monomeric WT actin is 56.77 ± 0.24°C.
source: Thermal denaturation temperatures (TM) analyzed by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) gave values of 56.77 ± 0.24°C and 56.19 ± 0.30°C for monomeric WT actin and p.E334Q.
evidence: This is experimental data from DSF experiments shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The thermal denaturation temperature of monomeric p.E334Q is 56.19 ± 0.30°C.
source: Thermal denaturation temperatures (TM) analyzed by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) gave values of 56.77 ± 0.24°C and 56.19 ± 0.30°C for monomeric WT actin and p.E334Q.
evidence: This is experimental data from DSF experiments shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The thermal denaturation temperature of WT filaments is 65.00 ± 0.76°C.
source: The values obtained for WT and E334Q filaments were 65.00 ± 0.76°C and 64.83 ± 0.25°C, respectively (Figure 1C, Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from DSF experiments shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The thermal denaturation temperature of E334Q filaments is 64.83 ± 0.25°C.
source: The values obtained for WT and E334Q filaments were 65.00 ± 0.76°C and 64.83 ± 0.25°C, respectively (Figure 1C, Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from DSF experiments shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The mutant actin is correctly folded.
source: Overall, these results show that the mutant actin is correctly folded and has comparable stability to the WT protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on DNase I inhibition, CD spectroscopy, and DSF data.

claim: The mutant actin has comparable stability to the WT protein.
source: Overall, these results show that the mutant actin is correctly folded and has comparable stability to the WT protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on DSF data showing similar denaturation temperatures.

claim: Mutations in the hinge region do not necessarily affect protein stability.
source: Our biochemical analysis shows that the mutation does not affect the folding of the actin monomer or the stability of the monomer and the resulting filaments, demonstrating that mutations in the hinge region do not necessarily affect protein stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data for E334Q.

claim: The mutant protein displays a robust interaction with the VCA-activated Arp2/3 complex.
source: The mutant protein displays a robust interaction with the VCA-activated Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy and pyrene-based polymerization assays shown in Figure 2D, E, F.

claim: p.E334Q polymerization kinetics are equivalent to those of the WT protein.
source: Its polymerization kinetics are equivalent to those of the WT protein, with which it effectively copolymerizes in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy and pyrene-based polymerization assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: p.E334Q effectively copolymerizes with WT protein in vitro.
source: Its polymerization kinetics are equivalent to those of the WT protein, with which it effectively copolymerizes in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with 1:1 mixtures shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Functional haploinsufficiency is excluded as a potential disease mechanism for E334Q.
source: Based on these observations, we exclude functional haploinsufficiency as a potential disease mechanism and favor a mechanism in which p.E334Q integrates into the cytoskeletal actin networks of the cell but shows defects in the interaction with key binding partners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing normal folding, stability, and polymerization.

claim: p.E334Q integrates into the cytoskeletal actin networks of the cell but shows defects in the interaction with key binding partners.
source: Based on these observations, we exclude functional haploinsufficiency as a potential disease mechanism and favor a mechanism in which p.E334Q integrates into the cytoskeletal actin networks of the cell but shows defects in the interaction with key binding partners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing normal polymerization but altered interactions with myosin and cofilin.

claim: Actin residue E334 interacts with a positively charged patch in the cardiomyopathy loop (CM-loop) of the myosin upper 50 kDa domain of NM2C and Myo5A.
source: Actin residue E334 interacts with a positively charged patch in the cardiomyopathy loop (CM-loop) of the myosin upper 50 kDa domain of NM2C and Myo5A (Pospich et al., 2021; von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited in the manuscript and shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the case of NM2C, the electrostatic interaction of E334 with K429 in the CM loop is further stabilized by van der Waals interactions with I420 and V427.
source: In the case of NM2C, the electrostatic interaction of E334 with K429 in the CM loop is further stabilized by van der Waals interactions with I420 and V427 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A lysine residue corresponding to K429 in NM2C is present in all human myosin-2 and myosin-5 isoforms.
source: A lysine residue corresponding to K429 in NM2C is present in all human myosin-2 and myosin-5 isoforms.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mutation E334Q in cytoskeletal γ-actin leads to the weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions in the actomyosin interface.
source: During force-generating interactions with mutant actin filaments, the weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions in this region of the actomyosin interface is likely to attenuate the binding affinity of class 2 and 5 myosins as well as the coupling between their actin and nucleotide-binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by experimental data showing reduced affinity.

claim: The weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions is likely to attenuate the binding affinity of class 2 and 5 myosins.
source: During force-generating interactions with mutant actin filaments, the weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions in this region of the actomyosin interface is likely to attenuate the binding affinity of class 2 and 5 myosins as well as the coupling between their actin and nucleotide-binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by experimental data showing reduced affinity (Figure 8, Table 1).

claim: The weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions is likely to attenuate the coupling between actin and nucleotide-binding sites in class 2 and 5 myosins.
source: During force-generating interactions with mutant actin filaments, the weakening of complementary electrostatic interactions in this region of the actomyosin interface is likely to attenuate the binding affinity of class 2 and 5 myosins as well as the coupling between their actin and nucleotide-binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by experimental data showing reduced coupling efficiency (Table 1).

claim: Cytoskeletal γ-actin filaments move with an average sliding velocity of 195.3 ± 5.0 nm s–1 on lawns of surface-immobilized NM2A-HMM molecules.
source: Cytoskeletal γ-actin filaments move with an average sliding velocity of 195.3 ± 5.0 nm s–1 on lawns of surface-immobilized NM2A-HMM molecules (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro motility assays shown in Figure 8A, B and Table 1.

claim: Filaments formed by p.E334Q actin move fivefold slower on NM2A-HMM, resulting in an observed average sliding velocity of 39.1 ± 3.2 nm s–1.
source: Filaments formed by p.E334Q actin move fivefold slower, resulting in an observed average sliding velocity of 39.1 ± 3.2 nm s–1.
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro motility assays shown in Figure 8A, B and Table 1.

claim: Filaments copolymerized from a 1:1 mixture of WT and p.E334Q actin move with an average sliding velocity of 131.2 ± 10 nm s–1 on NM2A-HMM.
source: Filaments copolymerized from a 1:1 mixture of WT and p.E334Q actin move with an average sliding velocity of 131.2 ± 10 nm s–1 (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from in vitro motility assays shown in Figure 8A, B and Table 1.

claim: The number of rapid dissociation and association events increased markedly for p.E334Q filaments compared to WT filaments in motility assays.
source: When equal densities of surface-attached WT and mutant filaments were used, we observed that the number of rapid dissociation and association events increased markedly for p.E334Q filaments (Figure 8—videos 1–3).
evidence: This is observational data from in vitro motility assays.

claim: The value for KDA/KD obtained for the interaction of NM2A-2R in the presence of p.E334Q (20.9) is 3.5-fold lower than the value measured in the presence of WT actin.
source: The coupling efficiency is given by the ratio of the dissociation equilibrium constants for actin binding in the absence (KA) and presence of ADP (KDA). The value for KDA/KD obtained for the interaction of NM2A-2R in the presence of p.E334Q (20.9) is 3.5-fold lower than the value measured in the presence of WT actin (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Reduced allosteric coupling between the actin- and nucleotide-binding sites within the myosin motor domain contributes to the observed decrease in motor activity with p.E334Q.
source: The results from our transient kinetic analysis of the complexes formed by p.E334Q with NM2A-2R indicate that reduced allosteric coupling between the actin- and nucleotide-binding sites within the myosin motor domain contributes to the observed decrease in motor activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transient kinetic data showing reduced coupling efficiency.

claim: Cofilin-1 binds to actin filaments by making simultaneous contact with two adjacent monomers.
source: Cofilin-1 binds to actin filaments by making simultaneous contact with two adjacent monomers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cofilin binding, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Actin residue E334 is located halfway between two adjacent cofilin molecules.
source: Actin residue E334 is located halfway between two adjacent cofilin molecules, but only makes direct contact with residue L111 of the cofilin-1 molecule on the pointed end side (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Actin residue E334 only makes direct contact with residue L111 of the cofilin-1 molecule on the pointed end side.
source: Actin residue E334 is located halfway between two adjacent cofilin molecules, but only makes direct contact with residue L111 of the cofilin-1 molecule on the pointed end side (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Cofilin-1 residue L111 is located in an α-helix (L111-L128) that is essential for actin binding.
source: Cofilin-1 residue L111 is located in an α-helix (L111-L128) that is essential for actin binding (Pope et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mutation E334Q maintains the van der Waals interaction with L111.
source: Mutation E334Q maintains the van der Waals interaction with L111, but reduces the electrostatic attraction between the interacting surfaces, with likely effects on the stability and allosteric coupling of the complex (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mutation E334Q reduces the electrostatic attraction between the actin-cofilin interacting surfaces.
source: Mutation E334Q maintains the van der Waals interaction with L111, but reduces the electrostatic attraction between the interacting surfaces, with likely effects on the stability and allosteric coupling of the complex (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutation E334Q has likely effects on the stability and allosteric coupling of the actin-cofilin complex.
source: Mutation E334Q maintains the van der Waals interaction with L111, but reduces the electrostatic attraction between the interacting surfaces, with likely effects on the stability and allosteric coupling of the complex (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Substantial changes in the low-frequency modes associated with global conformational changes were observed when comparing the partially cofilin-decorated filaments of WT and mutant filaments.
source: Substantial changes in the low-frequency modes associated with global conformational changes were observed when comparing the partially cofilin-decorated filaments of WT and mutant filaments, where the bare and cofilin-decorated regions move as rigid bodies and the interface between the two regions acts as a hinge (modes 7, 8) or fulcrum (mode 9) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on normal mode analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In experiments with p.E334Q-actin, de novo filament nucleation proceeded faster in the presence of cofilin-1.
source: In experiments with p.E334Q-actin, de novo filament nucleation proceeded faster (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of cofilin, the changes in pyrene fluorescence are best described by single exponential functions with kobs values of 0.0022 ± 0.0002 s–1 and 0.0029 ± 0.0003 s–1 for WT and p.E334Q filaments, respectively.
source: In the absence of cofilin, the changes in pyrene fluorescence are best described by single exponential functions with kobs values of 0.0022 ± 0.0002 s–1 and 0.0029 ± 0.0003 s–1 for WT and p.E334Q filaments, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the highest cofilin-1 concentration used (40 nM), the change in pyrene fluorescence with p.E334Q filaments is best described by a single exponential function with a kobs value of 0.0059 ± 0.0008 s–1.
source: At the highest cofilin-1 concentration used (40 nM), the change in pyrene fluorescence with p.E334Q filaments is still best described by a single exponential function with a kobs value of 0.0059 ± 0.0008 s–1.
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays.

claim: At 40 nM cofilin-1, the change in pyrene fluorescence for WT filaments is best fitted to a bi-exponential function with kobs values for the fast and slow phases of 0.0163 ± 0.0028 s–1 and 0.0002 ± 0.00003 s–1, respectively.
source: In contrast, the change for WT filaments is best fitted to a bi-exponential function. Here, the kobs values for the fast and slow phases are 0.0163 ± 0.0028 s–1 and 0.0002 ± 0.00003 s–1, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In experiments performed with p.E334Q filaments, the value obtained for kC was 4.2-fold lower (0.81 × 10–4 ± 0.08 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1) compared to experiments with WT filaments (3.42 × 10–4 ± 0.22 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1).
source: In experiments performed with p.E334Q filaments, the value obtained for kC was 4.2-fold lower (0.81 × 10–4 ± 0.08 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1) compared to experiments with WT filaments (3.42 × 10–4 ± 0.22 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1).
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: When heterofilaments were used, the effect of the mutation was reduced to a 2.2-fold difference compared to WT filaments (1.54 × 10–4 ± 0.11 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1).
source: When heterofilaments were used, the effect of the mutation was reduced to a 2.2-fold difference compared to WT filaments (1.54 × 10–4 ± 0.11 × 10–4 nM–1 s–1).
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays shown in Table 1.

claim: Cofilin-1 binds to and disassembles p.E334Q and WT filaments at pH 6.5.
source: This endpoint experiment showed that cofilin-1 binds to and disassembles p.E334Q and WT filaments (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Most pellet fractions from the experiments conducted with WT filaments were found to contain less cofilin-1 as higher disassembly efficiency results in more cofilin-1 being bound to actin monomers and retained in the supernatant fraction.
source: Most pellet fractions from the experiments conducted with WT filaments were found to contain less cofilin-1 as higher disassembly efficiency results in more cofilin-1 being bound to actin monomers and retained in the supernatant fraction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The shift to pH 7.8 did not have the same enhancing effect on the disassembly of p.E334Q filaments, as indicated by an increase in p.E334Q actin in the pellet fraction.
source: The shift to pH 7.8 did not have the same enhancing effect on the disassembly of p.E334Q filaments, as indicated by an increase in p.E334Q actin in the pellet fraction.
evidence: This is experimental data from co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The endpoint measurements show that cofilin-1 binds to p.E334Q filaments but severs them less efficiently.
source: The endpoint measurements show that cofilin-1 binds to p.E334Q filaments but severs them less efficiently.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from co-sedimentation assays.

claim: The dissociation equilibrium constant for binding of cofilin-1 to p.E334Q filaments is KD, p.E334Q = 1.83 ± 0.13 µM.
source: Fitting a quadratic equation to the obtained experimental values gave only slightly different dissociation equilibrium constants of KD, p.E334Q = 1.83 ± 0.13 µM and KD, WT = 1.61 ± 0.07 µM (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is experimental data from fluorescence quench experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The dissociation equilibrium constant for binding of cofilin-1 to WT filaments is KD, WT = 1.61 ± 0.07 µM.
source: Fitting a quadratic equation to the obtained experimental values gave only slightly different dissociation equilibrium constants of KD, p.E334Q = 1.83 ± 0.13 µM and KD, WT = 1.61 ± 0.07 µM (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is experimental data from fluorescence quench experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At the end of the experimental dead time, almost twice as many cofilin clusters had formed in the field of view on WT filaments (151 ± 29) as on p.E334Q filaments (82 ± 6).
source: At the end of the experimental dead time, almost twice as many cofilin clusters had formed in the field of view on WT filaments (151 ± 29) as on p.E334Q filaments (82 ± 6) (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is experimental data from two-color TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At the end of the experimental dead time, the number of both WT and mutant actin filaments had doubled from initially about 95 to about 200 filaments.
source: the number of both WT and mutant actin filaments had doubled from initially about 95 to about 200 filaments (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is experimental data from two-color TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At the end of the experimental dead time, the Atto 655 fluorescence of the WT filaments had decreased to 30% of the starting value, whereas the Atto 655 fluorescence of p.E334Q filaments remained unchanged.
source: and the Atto 655 fluorescence of the WT filaments had decreased to 30% of the starting value, whereas the Atto 655 fluorescence of p.E334Q filaments remained unchanged (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is experimental data from two-color TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 6C.

claim: During the following 500 s, total eGFP-cofilin-1 fluorescence increased linearly, with the rate of increase being approximately twice as fast for WT as for p.E334Q filaments.
source: During the following 500 s, total eGFP-cofilin-1 fluorescence increased linearly, with the rate of increase being approximately twice as fast for WT as for p.E334Q filaments (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is experimental data from two-color TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No severing events were observed with fully decorated filaments.
source: No severing events were observed with fully decorated filaments.
evidence: This is observational data from two-color TIRF microscopy experiments.

claim: The mutation affects cofilin-mediated nucleation and severing in opposite ways.
source: Our results show that the mutation affects these different cofilin functions in actin dynamics in opposite ways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data showing increased nucleation but decreased severing.

claim: Cofilin-mediated filament nucleation is more efficient for p.E334Q monomers.
source: Cofilin-mediated filament nucleation is more efficient for p.E334Q monomers, while cofilin-mediated severing of filaments containing p.E334Q is significantly reduced.
evidence: This is experimental data from TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cofilin-mediated severing of filaments containing p.E334Q is significantly reduced.
source: Cofilin-mediated filament nucleation is more efficient for p.E334Q monomers, while cofilin-mediated severing of filaments containing p.E334Q is significantly reduced.
evidence: This is experimental data from pyrene-based depolymerization assays and two-color TIRF microscopy shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The E334Q mutation leads to a 5-fold reduction in sliding velocity of actin filaments on NM2A-HMM.
source: Filaments formed by p.E334Q actin move fivefold slower, resulting in an observed average sliding velocity of 39.1 ± 3.2 nm s–1.
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of WT (195.3 nm/s) to mutant (39.1 nm/s) sliding velocities.

claim: The E334Q mutation leads to a 9.9-fold reduction in affinity of NM2A-2R for actin under rigor conditions.
source: The values measured under rigor conditions show a 9.9-fold reduced affinity of NM2A-2R for p.E334Q filaments (KA = 16.9 ± 1.3 nM) compared to WT filaments (KA = 1.7 ± 0.3 nM) (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of mutant to WT KA values.

claim: Typical yields of purified protein ranged from 5 to 7 mg for cytoskeletal γ-actin and p.E334Q starting with 2 × 10^9 cells.
source: Starting with 2 × 109 cells, typical yields ranged from 5 to 7 mg of purified protein for cytoskeletal γ-actin and p.E334Q (N = 3 for WT and N = 4 for p.E334Q) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from protein production and purification.

claim: The nucleotide dissociation rate k-T for p.E334Q-actin is about 2-fold faster than for WT monomers.
source: With p.E334Q-actin, we observed rates of k-T = 0.0972 ± 0.0019 s–1 and k-D = 0.3199 ± 0.0027 s–1. These rates are about 2-fold and 1.5-fold faster than those observed in experiments performed with WT monomers (k-T = 0.0473 ± 0.0013 s–1, k-D = 0.2155 ± 0.0017 s–1; Figure 1D, Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from nucleotide exchange assays shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: The nucleotide dissociation rate k-D for p.E334Q-actin is about 1.5-fold faster than for WT monomers.
source: With p.E334Q-actin, we observed rates of k-T = 0.0972 ± 0.0019 s–1 and k-D = 0.3199 ± 0.0027 s–1. These rates are about 2-fold and 1.5-fold faster than those observed in experiments performed with WT monomers (k-T = 0.0473 ± 0.0013 s–1, k-D = 0.2155 ± 0.0017 s–1; Figure 1D, Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from nucleotide exchange assays shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: TIRF microscopy-based tracking revealed a small but significant reduction in the elongation rate from 12.6 ± 0.3 nm s–1 for WT to 11.1 ± 0.3 nm s–1 for mutant filaments.
source: Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy-based tracking of the polymerization of monomeric Atto 655-labeled WT or mutant actin in vitro revealed a small but significant reduction in the elongation rate from 12.6 ± 0.3 nm s–1 for WT to 11.1 ± 0.3 nm s–1 for mutant filaments (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: p.E334Q shows only a mild polymerization defect.
source: Overall, p.E334Q shows only a mild polymerization defect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data showing small reductions in elongation rate but normal nucleation.

claim: The E334Q mutation is likely to affect the interaction of mutant filaments with Myo1D, Myo1G, NM2B, Myo5B, Myo5C, and Myo19 due to the presence of the core contact triad residues in their CM loops.
source: Analogous changes in the interaction of mutant filaments with Myo1D, Myo1G, NM2B, Myo5B, Myo5C, and Myo19 are expected due to the presence of the core contact triad residues in their CM loops (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The absence of a basic residue corresponding to K429 in NM2C makes it difficult to predict the consequences for the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with certain cytoskeletal myosin isoforms.
source: In contrast, the absence of a basic residue corresponding to K429 in NM2C and additional changes affecting their CM loop structure make it difficult to predict the consequences for the interaction of p.E334Q filaments with the cytoskeletal myosin isoforms Myo1A, Myo1C, Myo1E, Myo1F, Myo3A, Myo3B, Myo15, Myo18A, Myo18B, and Myo19.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis.

claim: The E334Q mutation slows the initial complex formation with cofilin due to less favorable charge interactions.
source: Our results are consistent with the E334Q mutation slowing the initial complex formation due to less favorable charge interactions and allosteric perturbations having a major impact on subsequent steps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from cofilin binding and severing assays.

claim: Allosteric perturbations have a major impact on subsequent steps in cofilin-actin interactions.
source: Our results are consistent with the E334Q mutation slowing the initial complex formation due to less favorable charge interactions and allosteric perturbations having a major impact on subsequent steps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from cofilin binding and severing assays.

claim: Patients carrying mutations in ACTB or ACTG1 predominately suffer from developmental disabilities.
source: Patients carrying mutations in ACTB or ACTG1 predominately suffer from developmental disabilities, which can be directly linked to cortical malformations of varying severity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Verloes et al., 2015; Di Donato et al., 2016; Rivière et al., 2012).

claim: Developmental disabilities in patients with ACTB or ACTG1 mutations can be directly linked to cortical malformations of varying severity.
source: Patients carrying mutations in ACTB or ACTG1 predominately suffer from developmental disabilities, which can be directly linked to cortical malformations of varying severity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Verloes et al., 2015; Di Donato et al., 2016; Rivière et al., 2012).

claim: Neuronal cells and/or neuronal progenitor cells are assumed to be the most affected cell population in patients with ACTB or ACTG1 mutations.
source: Therefore, neuronal cells and/or neuronal progenitor cells are assumed to be the most affected cell population in the patients (Verloes et al., 2015; Di Donato et al., 2016; Rivière et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical phenotypes and is supported by citations.

claim: The actin composition of the neuron is thought to reach ratios between 1:1 and 1:2 for γ-actin to β-actin in the mature state after fluctuations during neuronal development.
source: The actin composition of the neuron is thought to reach ratios between 1:1 and 1:2 for γ-actin to β-actin in the mature state after fluctuations during neuronal development (Cheever and Ervasti, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: p.E334Q actin is readily produced and integrated into the cytoskeletal actin networks of neuronal cells.
source: Based on our results, we conclude that p.E334Q actin is readily produced and integrated into the cytoskeletal actin networks of neuronal cells, where it perturbs interactions with cytoskeletal myosin isoforms that play essential roles in the function and maintenance of healthy neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing normal folding, stability, and polymerization.

claim: p.E334Q actin perturbs interactions with cytoskeletal myosin isoforms that play essential roles in the function and maintenance of healthy neurons.
source: Based on our results, we conclude that p.E334Q actin is readily produced and integrated into the cytoskeletal actin networks of neuronal cells, where it perturbs interactions with cytoskeletal myosin isoforms that play essential roles in the function and maintenance of healthy neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing impaired myosin interactions and the known roles of myosins in neurons.

claim: The functions of myosin-5 isoforms in neuronal cells are all linked to their role as actin barbed-end-directed processive cargo transporters.
source: The functions of myosin-5 isoforms in neuronal cells are all linked to their role as actin barbed-end-directed processive cargo transporters (Hammer and Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Several of the myosin-5-driven transport processes are important contributors to synaptic plasticity.
source: Several of the myosin-5-driven transport processes are important contributors to synaptic plasticity, that is, the ability of the neurons to change synaptic strength based on previous activities (Hammer and Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NM2A is predominately enriched in the vasculature of the brain.
source: NM2A is predominately enriched in the vasculature of the brain, consistent with the importance of NM2A for angiogenesis (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NM2B and NM2C are mainly found in growth cones and dendritic spines of neuronal cells.
source: NM2B and NM2C are mainly found in growth cones and dendritic spines of neuronal cells (Murakami and Elzinga, 1992; Golomb et al., 2004; Rochlin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NM2B was shown to determine the maturation and morphology of the dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons.
source: NM2B was shown to determine the maturation and morphology of the dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons and was additionally linked to basal synaptic function and plasticity (Hodges et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2004; Rex et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NM2B was linked to basal synaptic function and plasticity.
source: NM2B was shown to determine the maturation and morphology of the dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons and was additionally linked to basal synaptic function and plasticity (Hodges et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2004; Rex et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NM2C and NM2B contribute to the differentiation of oligodendrocytes.
source: NM2C and NM2B contribute to the differentiation of oligodendrocytes (Domingues et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The NM2 isoforms compete with proteins of the ADF/cofilin family for binding to F-actin.
source: The NM2 isoforms compete with proteins of the ADF/cofilin family for binding to F-actin, and this competition is essential for stable actomyosin contractility and an intact cell cortex (Wiggan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Competition between NM2 isoforms and ADF/cofilin family proteins is essential for stable actomyosin contractility and an intact cell cortex.
source: The NM2 isoforms compete with proteins of the ADF/cofilin family for binding to F-actin, and this competition is essential for stable actomyosin contractility and an intact cell cortex (Wiggan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ADF/cofilin family members are highly abundant in growth cones and dendritic spines.
source: In line with this, ADF/cofilin family members are highly abundant in growth cones and dendritic spines and essential for spine morphology and determination of spine length by modulating actin turnover (Star et al., 2002; Hotulainen et al., 2009; Namme et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ADF/cofilin family members are essential for spine morphology and determination of spine length by modulating actin turnover.
source: In line with this, ADF/cofilin family members are highly abundant in growth cones and dendritic spines and essential for spine morphology and determination of spine length by modulating actin turnover (Star et al., 2002; Hotulainen et al., 2009; Namme et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cofilin-mediated severing and nucleation were previously proposed to synergistically contribute to global actin turnover in cells.
source: Cofilin-mediated severing and nucleation were previously proposed to synergistically contribute to global actin turnover in cells (Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006; Du and Frieden, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations of residue E334 in α-skeletal actin are reported to result in nemaline myopathy (E334K) or core myopathy (E334A).
source: Mutations of residue E334 in α-skeletal actin (encoded by ACTA1) are reported to result in nemaline myopathy (E334K; Laing et al., 2009) or core myopathy (E334A; Kaindl et al., 2004; reviewed in Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of charge at actin residue 334 leads to the loss of a conserved core contact between actin and the myosin motor domain of cytoskeletal class 2 myosin.
source: Our study shows that loss of charge at actin residue 334 leads to the loss of a conserved core contact between actin and the myosin motor domain of cytoskeletal class 2 myosin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and structural analysis.

claim: Mutations of residue E334 in α-skeletal actin likely affect the interaction with skeletal muscle myosin-2 to a similar extent as observed with cytoskeletal γ-actin.
source: Because the core contact triad that interacts with actin residue E334 is present in all class 2 myosin isoforms, it is reasonable to assume that mutations of residue E334 in α-skeletal actin affect the interaction with skeletal muscle myosin-2 to a similar extent, resulting in less efficient force generation and thereby contributing to the development of myopathy in patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation and the experimental data with cytoskeletal γ-actin.

claim: Mutations in ACTB and ACTG1 are associated with lymphoid cancers.
source: Interestingly, a recent study analyzing the prevalence of cytoskeletal actin mutations in cancer using the cBioPortal database found that mutations in ACTB and ACTG1 are associated with lymphoid cancers, specifically mutations in ACTB with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and mutations in ACTG1 with multiple myeloma.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation (Witjes et al., 2020).

claim: Residue E334 in ACTB is identified as a potential hotspot as the missense variants p.E334Q/p.E334K are more frequent in cancer datasets.
source: Nevertheless, the group identified residue E334 in ACTB as a potential hotspot as the missense variants p.E334Q/p.E334K are more frequent in all analyzed datasets (Witjes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The high sequence similarity between the cytoskeletal actin isoforms makes it highly likely that the E334Q mutation in cytoskeletal β-actin results in similar molecular perturbations of actin dynamics.
source: However, the high sequence similarity between the cytoskeletal actin isoforms makes it highly likely that the E334Q mutation in cytoskeletal β-actin results in similar molecular perturbations of actin dynamics but with potentially different consequences for the organism due to varying enrichment of the two isoforms in functional compartments of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity and the experimental data with γ-actin.
